logbook.turtle.name: Green turtle
logbook.turtle.facts: Green turtles eat seagrass and algae. Lost fishing nets can trap them, and they can swallow plastic. In 2025 their IUCN status improved from Endangered (EN) to Least Concern (LC), but their numbers are still far below past levels.
logbook.turtle.sdg: Target 14.1 calls for preventing and significantly reducing marine pollution, including marine debris.
logbook.reefShark.name: Blacktip reef shark
logbook.reefShark.facts: Blacktip reef sharks live in shallow water near coral reefs, and their fin tips are black. Fishers catch them with nets and lines, mostly as bycatch. Their numbers are falling, and the IUCN listed them as Vulnerable (VU) in 2020.
logbook.reefShark.sdg: Target 14.4 calls for regulating fishing and ending overfishing, so fish stocks can recover.
logbook.clownfish.name: Clownfish
logbook.clownfish.facts: Clownfish live among the tentacles of sea anemones on sheltered reefs and lagoons. They grow to 11 cm at most. The IUCN rated them Least Concern (LC) in 2021, but they are collected for aquariums and their host anemones can bleach.
logbook.clownfish.sdg: Target 14.2 calls for protecting marine and coastal ecosystems, strengthening their resilience, and restoring them.
logbook.mantaRay.name: Reef manta ray
logbook.mantaRay.facts: Reef manta rays can be over 4 metres wide and eat plankton. The IUCN rated them Vulnerable (VU) in 2018, because their gills are traded and fishers often catch them. Indonesia has fully protected them since 2014.
logbook.mantaRay.sdg: Target 14.4 calls for regulating fishing and ending overfishing, including illegal fishing.
logbook.dolphin.name: Spinner dolphin
logbook.dolphin.facts: Spinner dolphins are known for leaping and spinning in the air. In the daytime they often rest in shallow water near shore. The IUCN rated them Least Concern (LC) in 2018, but they can get tangled in or swallow marine debris, and are often caught as bycatch.
logbook.dolphin.sdg: Target 14.1 calls for preventing and significantly reducing marine pollution, including marine debris.
logbook.coral.name: Coral
logbook.coral.facts: Corals are invertebrate animals, related to jellyfish and sea anemones. Reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but support about 25% of marine creatures. More acidic seawater can make it harder for corals to build their skeletons.
logbook.coral.sdg: Target 14.3 calls for minimizing and addressing the impacts of ocean acidification, including through scientific cooperation.
logbook.seagrass.name: Seagrass
logbook.seagrass.facts: Seagrasses are flowering plants that live underwater in shallow seas, not algae. Seagrass meadows cover only 0.1% of the ocean floor, yet they are nurseries for fish and turtles and store up to 18% of ocean carbon. Runoff and coastal building can damage them.
logbook.seagrass.sdg: Target 14.2 calls for protecting marine and coastal ecosystems, and restoring them when damaged.

mission.title: Mission: Restore the Bay
mission.state: The bay is murky and its corals are bleaching. About {trash} pieces of trash lie on the sea floor, float on the surface and litter the beach. {nets} ghost nets have trapped a turtle and a reef shark.
mission.1: Clean the bay to {percent}%, then drop the trash off at the recycling shed on land.
mission.2: Cut the ghost nets to free the turtle and the reef shark.
mission.3: Set up {frames} reef frames, shoot coral fragments onto them, and plant seagrass seeds in {patches} patches.
mission.4: Once the bay is clear again, scan {entries} kinds of sea life for the Marine Logbook.
